display_name: Wind Gap Woodruff Vineyard Pinot Noir, Santa Cruz Mountains
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Woodruff Vineyard Pinot Noir comes from steep, thin shale-and-sandstone soils high in the Santa Cruz Mountains fog belt, and that site-driven minerality and bright acidity define the wine more than overt California ripeness. The result is a lithe, iron-tinged Pinot that reads of mountains and ocean breezes rather than tropical fruit.",
  "wine_summary": "This bottling matters because it isolates a single-vineyard voice from an AVA where elevation and fog create sharp contrasts across short distances. Wind Gap focuses on cool-climate, site-specific expressions; the Woodruff Vineyard fruit carries the hallmarks of the Santa Cruz Mountains—fog-suffused mornings, strong diurnal shift, and shallow, fast-draining soils that concentrate flavor and acidity. Those elements produce Pinot Noir with restrained red fruit, savory herbs, and a mineral thread tied to fractured shale and iron-rich soils.",
  "terroir_expression": "Shale and sandstone underlain by pockets of decomposed granite force vines to struggle for water and root into fractured rock; that struggle concentrates phenolics and produces a taut acid backbone. Morning marine fog from the Pacific delays ripening, preserving bright cranberry and red cherry notes while afternoon sun ripens phenolic maturity—together creating a Pinot with juicy fruit framed by saline-iron minerality and a nervy finish.",
  "vinification_summary": "Specific winemaking notes for these vintages are limited; producers in the Santa Cruz Mountains making single-vineyard Pinot commonly use small-lot fermentations, careful temperature control and a mix of de-stemmed and partial whole-cluster fermentation to balance fruit and structure. Whole-cluster fermentation (fermenting intact grape clusters including stems) can add stem tannin and lift, contributing spicy, transparent structure without heavy oak; neutral or light-toast French oak is typically used to avoid masking the site's minerality.",
  "food_pairing": [
    "Nashville hot chicken with pickles and white bread — the wine's bright acidity cuts fat and its red-fruit spice complements the heat.",
    "Wood-fired wild mushroom pizza with fontina and thyme — earthy, umami mushrooms echo the Pinot's savory edge and mineral notes.",
    "Seared duck breast with cherry-garlic gastrique and roasted baby carrots — the wine's cranberry-cherry core and acid balance the duck's richness and sweet-sour glaze.",
    "Charred sockeye salmon with miso-butter and scallions — the saline mineral thread and bright acidity hold up to umami and slight oiliness without overpowering the fish."
  ],
  "comparable_wines": "Windy Oaks Estate Pinot Noir — comparable because it is drawn from the same Santa Cruz Mountains fog influence and often shows similar shale-driven minerality. Thomas Fogarty Vineyards Pinot Noir — comparable for its high-elevation, cool-climate profile and emphasis on acidity and mountain tannic structure.",
  "style_profile": "Pinot Noir — medium-bodied with lively acidity and an iron-rich mineral finish",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink now through 2028 for freshness and savory notes; store at 55°F and open or decant 20–30 minutes to let tertiary aromatics emerge. If well kept, the best bottles can maintain interest for another 3–5 years.",
  "value_assessment": "Price: $45–65 retail. Competitors at this price include Windy Oaks Estate Pinot Noir ($40–60) and Thomas Fogarty Reserve Pinot Noir ($50–80). This is worth buying if you prioritize site-specific, cool-climate Pinots with mineral tension rather than riper, oak-driven California Pinot; it competes well on terroir clarity for the mid-market mountain-Pinot segment.",
  "market_position": "This wine fits boutique retail shops, mountain-focused wine lists, and collectors who seek single-vineyard California Pinot rather than mass-market examples. Expect to see it on corkage-friendly neighborhood restaurants and specialized lists where sommeliers highlight AVA-driven differences.",
  "insider_take": "Unlike many California Pinots that chase ripeness, the Woodruff bottling emphasizes minerality and acid; buyers who want jammy fruit should skip it. If you collect Santa Cruz Mountains sites or build a tasting flight of mountain Pinots, this bottle is a strong buy for its clear sense of place and textural tension.",
